headline: New Zealand Parliament Passes India Trade Deal and Contested Policing and Youth Justice Laws
summary: During an extended sitting, Parliament passed the India free-trade agreement legislation, new move-on powers for police, youth justice reforms and changes to local government law. Government members argued the measures would support exporters, public safety and cost-effective services, while opponents warned of risks to household welfare, civil liberties, Māori participation and the rights of vulnerable people. Question time also exposed continuing disputes over grocery prices, benefit payment failures and health workforce claims.

topicSummaries.topic: Grocery Prices and Supermarket Competition Remain a Cost-of-Living Flashpoint
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: Food prices affect every household, and MPs disputed whether the Government’s competition measures are doing enough to ease grocery costs.
topicSummaries.content: Labour’s Arena Williams challenged Commerce and Consumer Affairs Minister Cameron Brewer over grocery prices and the Government’s response to supermarket market power. Brewer said annual food inflation was 1.9 percent in the year to July 2026, compared with 12.5 percent in the year to June 2023, and pointed to Commerce Commission enforcement and competition reforms. Opposition MPs cited price increases for some staples and questioned repeated reviews of the supermarket sector. The Government also referred to an independent analysis estimating that restructuring Foodstuffs could benefit households by $200 to $1,300 a year at full rollout; no final structural decision was recorded in the debate.

keyExchanges.speaker: Arena Williams (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: Are the supermarkets gouging New Zealanders, or is he telling the people who are worried about the price increases of 88 percent for butter, 33 percent for milk, and 31 percent for lamb, since his Government took office, to “cry me a river”, like his Prime Minister?

keyExchanges.speaker: Cameron Brewer (National)
keyExchanges.quote: As I have repeated said, and I will repeat again, New Zealanders pay too much for their groceries, and that is why we are doing the work that I just outlined.

topicSummaries.topic: MSD Processing Delays Affected 2,460 Benefit Recipients
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: Delayed payments left thousands without benefits they were entitled to, and the Minister acknowledged that the failures caused hardship.
topicSummaries.content: Labour and Green MPs questioned Social Development Minister Louise Upston about Ministry of Social Development processing delays linked to its Confirming Your Circumstances reviews. Upston said 2,460 main-benefit clients were affected, including 2,349 people receiving the Supported Living Payment; the Ministry did not separate suspensions from cancellations. She said payments had been reinstated and arrears paid, and acknowledged that people experienced harm and hardship. A review released the previous week identified failures and recommendations, which the Minister said she expected the Ministry to implement promptly. The Speaker declined a request for another urgent debate on the report, saying the House had already debated the circumstances.

keyExchanges.speaker: Ricardo Menéndez March (Green)
keyExchanges.quote: Has she bothered to ask the Ministry for Social Development whether any of the sick, injured, or disabled New Zealanders who lost their main source of income went hungry, into debt, or became homeless?

keyExchanges.speaker: Louise Upston (National)
keyExchanges.quote: It is clear from the review that was undertaken that people went without payments that shouldn’t have, and I have acknowledged—as has the chief executive of MSD—that that has created harm and hardship, for which we have both apologised.

topicSummaries.topic: Health Debate Leaves Net Nurse Growth Unclear as Health NZ Plans a $475M Deficit
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The size of the nursing workforce and Health New Zealand’s funding affect access to care and the capacity of hospitals and other services.
topicSummaries.content: Labour’s Ayesha Verrall questioned Health Minister Simeon Brown about a reported structural funding gap and the Government’s claim that it was recruiting 2,300 nurses. Brown said the Government had agreed to allow Health New Zealand a projected $475 million deficit in 2026–27 to deliver more services, and described the spending as deliberate. On recruitment, he cited 2,378 full-time-equivalent roles being filled but did not commit to a net increase of 2,300 nurses, noting that turnover, retirements and other workforce movements affect the final total. The dispute continued later, with Labour arguing gross recruitment figures did not establish net workforce growth.

keyExchanges.speaker: Ayesha Verrall (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: Is the Government committing to a net growth of 2,300 nurses?

keyExchanges.speaker: Simeon Brown (National)
keyExchanges.quote: We’re committing to growing our workforce, filling vacancies, and ensuring that we are recruiting as we have been since we came to Government, with 2,100 additional nurses since we came to Government.

topicSummaries.topic: India Free-Trade Agreement Passes Third Reading Amid Investment and Migration Concerns
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The agreement changes the terms for exporters seeking access to India, while its investment and migration provisions carry implications for businesses and future governments.
topicSummaries.content: Parliament passed the India Free Trade Agreement Legislation Amendment Bill and the related India Export Quotas (Apples, Kiwifruit, and Mānuka Honey) Bill at third reading. Trade Minister Todd McClay said the agreement would reduce or eliminate tariffs on 95 percent of current exports to India, with 57 percent entering duty-free from the start and 82 percent once fully implemented. Labour supported the bills while saying it would have negotiated a different agreement and secured commitments on migrant-worker protections. New Zealand First and the Greens opposed them, raising concerns including a commitment to promote US$20 billion of investment in India over 15 years, intellectual property, and the agreement’s migration provisions. McClay said the agreement was expected to enter into force later in 2026.

keyExchanges.speaker: David Wilson (New Zealand First)
keyExchanges.quote: Why on earth—why on earth, then, are we investing New Zealand dollars—$32 billion—in their economy with no reciprocal agreement?

keyExchanges.speaker: Todd McClay (National)
keyExchanges.quote: From day one of entering into force, 57 percent of our current exports will enter India duty free.

topicSummaries.topic: Three Treaty-Reference Bills Introduced as MPs Dispute Their Effect
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: Changes to Treaty references could affect how public bodies interpret their legal obligations and the relationship between Māori and the Crown.
topicSummaries.content: The Government introduced bills to repeal, standardise or change the strength of Treaty references in legislation and sought urgency for their initial consideration and referral. In question time, Prime Minister Christopher Luxon defended the review as a way to make obligations clearer and more consistent. Māori and opposition MPs argued that the proposals would weaken protections and accountability, and questioned their timing during Māori Language Week. The transcript records the bills’ introduction and debate over their purpose; it does not record their final passage.

keyExchanges.speaker: Rawiri Waititi (Te Pāti Māori)
keyExchanges.quote: Why has this Government decided to erase or weaken Te Tiriti o Waitangi obligations across 19 pieces of legislation under urgency during te Wiki o Te Reo Māori, and does he accept that he is undermining Māori rights while the country is celebrating Māori culture?

keyExchanges.speaker: Christopher Luxon (National)
keyExchanges.quote: Most importantly, we’re making sure that everyone’s clear about their obligations, because we’re getting maximum clarity and consistency.

topicSummaries.topic: Local Government Law Narrows Council Priorities and Voting Rights
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The changes affect what councils must prioritise and who can vote on their committees, including arrangements involving Māori representatives and community experts.
topicSummaries.content: The Local Government (System Improvements) Amendment Bill passed its third reading. Local Government Minister Simon Watts said it would focus councils on cost-effective infrastructure, public services and regulatory functions, and improve democratic accountability by reserving committee votes for elected members. Labour, the Greens and Te Pāti Māori argued that removing the four wellbeings and restricting non-elected members’ votes would centralise decisions and weaken local and Māori participation. The late addition of changes to committee voting, including provisions affecting Auckland’s Houkura board, drew particular criticism because those amendments had not been considered through the earlier select committee process. Government and New Zealand First members supported the bill, citing rates pressures and the need for councils to prioritise spending.

keyExchanges.speaker: Simon Watts (National)
keyExchanges.quote: This is not about race. This is not about iwi Māori. This is about democracy.

keyExchanges.speaker: Willie Jackson (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: Why did this Minister not meet with the Auckland Independent Māori Statutory Board?

topicSummaries.topic: Move-on Orders Bill Passes Despite Objections Over Rough Sleeping and Begging
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The law gives police a new tool to order people from public places, with potential fines or imprisonment for non-compliance, including in circumstances involving homelessness.
topicSummaries.content: The Summary Offences (Move-on Orders) Amendment Bill passed its third reading after a contested debate and urgent committee stage. It allows police to direct people to leave a public place for up to 24 hours for specified conduct, including disorderly or threatening behaviour, obstruction, unreasonable begging and rough sleeping; refusing to comply can lead to a fine of up to $1,000 or up to three months’ imprisonment. The select committee received more than 7,500 submissions, most opposing the bill, and amended it to apply only to people aged 18 and over, clarify the begging test, and require annual reporting and a review after three years. Justice Minister Paul Goldsmith said the measure was intended to address disorder, not criminalise homelessness. Opponents said it could displace people without addressing the reasons they were homeless.

keyExchanges.speaker: Paul Goldsmith (National)
keyExchanges.quote: Move-on orders do not criminalise homelessness.

keyExchanges.speaker: Dan Rosewarne (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: If someone is sleeping rough tonight in Wellington, Christchurch, Auckland, Dunedin, or anywhere else in New Zealand, they will still be sleeping rough tomorrow

topicSummaries.topic: Youth Justice Bill Creates Military-Style Academy Orders
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The law establishes a new, court-ordered response for a small group of serious young offenders, raising questions about rehabilitation, safety and oversight.
topicSummaries.content: The Oranga Tamariki (Responding to Serious Youth Offending) Amendment Bill passed its third reading. It creates young serious offender declarations and allows Youth Courts to make military-style academy orders, combining structured activities, education, therapeutic support and transition planning. The Children’s Minister said the programme was intended as an intensive alternative for young people at risk of further serious offending. Labour, the Greens and Te Pāti Māori opposed the bill, questioning the evidence for boot-camp-style approaches and raising concerns about assaults reported in pilot programmes, the ability of young people to leave, and the use of force by approved providers. The Government said oversight and safeguards would apply, while most opposition amendments were rejected.

keyExchanges.speaker: Karen Chhour (National)
keyExchanges.quote: They won’t be able to opt out. Only a Youth Court can cancel the military-style academy order.

keyExchanges.speaker: Willow-Jean Prime (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: Can the Minister please point out to me where in the legislation a young person is able to initiate that and get that before a court to make a decision on their circumstances, in situations where they may have been subjected to abuse and assault

topicSummaries.topic: Public Works Changes Pass After Dispute Over Property Rights and Private Projects
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The bill changes how land can be acquired for infrastructure, a process that can affect homes, farms and community assets.
topicSummaries.content: The Public Works Amendment Bill passed its third reading after debate about the balance between infrastructure delivery and private landowners’ rights. Land Information Minister Mike Butterick said it modernised acquisition and compensation processes, introduced an incentive payment for early agreement, and created a faster recovery process for public works damaged in emergencies. Labour supported earlier stages but voted against the final bill, saying late changes and links to resource-management reforms could extend the process to projects with private as well as public benefits. The Greens also opposed it, citing concerns about Māori land and the potential reach of acquisition powers. The Minister said combined projects could only be public works and that network utility access would remain subject to ministerial approval.

keyExchanges.speaker: Mike Butterick (National)
keyExchanges.quote: This bill provides a more modern, workable, and balanced framework for acquiring land for public works.

keyExchanges.speaker: Arena Williams (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: The question here is: are we now making even more exclusions which limit the amount of buildings which will be registered, and end up having an area which is arguably highly vulnerable to seismic activity without any sensible protections.

topicSummaries.topic: Move-on Orders and Youth Justice Laws Pass as Parliament Debates Health and Safety
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The new measures affect police powers and youth justice, while unresolved debate over service capacity and safeguards remains central to their implementation.
topicSummaries.content: The sitting also included disputes over health staffing and funding. Labour challenged the Government’s claims about recruiting 2,300 nurses and the size of net workforce growth; the Health Minister cited 2,378 full-time-equivalent roles being recruited but said the net change would depend on normal workforce movements. The Government also confirmed an agreed $475 million projected Health New Zealand deficit for 2026–27, describing it as a deliberate choice to support more care. These exchanges took place alongside the passage of the move-on orders and youth justice bills, with opposition MPs arguing that enforcement measures cannot substitute for adequate housing, health and social support.

keyExchanges.speaker: Ayesha Verrall (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: Is the Government committing to a net growth of 2,300 nurses?

keyExchanges.speaker: Simeon Brown (National)
keyExchanges.quote: We’re committing to growing our workforce, filling vacancies, and ensuring that we are recruiting as we have been since we came to Government, with 2,100 additional nurses since we came to Government.

conclusion: Parliament advanced a wide legislative programme, but the central political tension remained whether public safety and economic efficiency justify measures that opponents say weaken protections for vulnerable people, Māori participation and individual rights.
